## Principal component anaylisis in diabetes data set

### Introduction

The data consist of 19 variables on 403 subjects from 1046 subjects who were interviewed in a study to understand the prevalence of obesity, diabetes, and other cardiovascular risk factors in central Virginia for African Americans. According to Dr John Hong, Diabetes Mellitus Type II (adult onset diabetes) is associated most strongly with obesity. The 403 subjects were the ones who were actually screened for diabetes. Glycosolated hemoglobin \> 7.0 is usually taken as a positive diagnosis of diabetes.

The aim of this micro-report is to establish if there are any determining factors for diabetes diagnosis. Only cholesterol, glucose level, HDL, ratio and glycosolated hemoglobin are considered to perform PCA.

### Loading the data & initializing the libraries

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("cowplot")
library("ggrepel")
```

We are going to be working with the diabetes data set. The objective of this micro-report is finding out which out of all the possible variables determine the possibility of diabetes.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
```

### Re-structuring the data

First, the relevant numerical columns are conserved. Also, a new column is created, to classify diabetes diagnoses based on the glycosolated hemoglobin threshold.

```{r}
diabetes <- diabetes |>
  select('chol', 'stab.glu', 'hdl', 'ratio', 'glyhb') |>
  mutate(diagnosis = case_when(
    glyhb >= 7 ~ "diabetic",
    glyhb < 7 ~ "not_diabetic"
  ))
```

### Analysis

#### Data in PC coordinates

```{r}
diabetes_clean <- diabetes |>
  drop_na()

pca_fit <- diabetes_clean |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  prcomp(scale = TRUE)

```

Using `broom::augment()`, we project the original samples onto the principal components (`.fittedPC1`, `.fittedPC2`) to explore how diabetic and non-diabetic individuals separate across the latent dimensions.

```{r}
pca_fit |>
  augment(diabetes_clean) |>
  ggplot(aes(.fittedPC1, .fittedPC2, color = diagnosis)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(diabetic = "#D55E00", not_diabetic = "#0072B2")
  ) +
  theme_half_open(12) +
  background_grid()
```

Non-diabetic subjects are tightly clustered around the centre-left of the plot, while diabetic subjects are more spread out and shifted towards positive PC1 values.

#### Rotation matrix

We extract the rotation matrix using `broom::tidy()` with `matrix = "rotation"` to inspect the contribution (loadings) of each clinical measurement to each principal component.

```{r}

pca_fit |> 
  tidy(matrix = "rotation")
```

```{r}
arrow_style <- arrow(
  angle = 20, ends = "first", type = "closed", length = grid::unit(8, "pt")
)

pca_fit |>
  tidy(matrix = "rotation") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = "PC", names_prefix = "PC", values_from = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_segment(xend = 0, yend = 0, arrow = arrow_style) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = column)) +
  xlim(-0.6, 0.7) +
  ylim(-0.5, 0.85) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal_grid(12)
```

Glycosolated hemoglobin (glyhb), stabilised glucose (stab.glu), cholesterol (chol) and ratio point towards positive PC1, the same direction in which diabetic subjects are located. HDL points in the opposite direction, so higher HDL is associated with the non-diabetic side. Glyhb, stab.glu and chol point in a similar direction, so they are correlated.

### Data Variability explained by PCs

```{r}
pca_fit %>%
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues")


```

```{r}
pca_fit %>%
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") %>%
  ggplot(aes(PC, percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  theme_minimal_hgrid(12)
```

We can see that the first PC explains 46% of the variance, PC1 and PC2 together explain 72%, and the first 3 principle components cover almost all variance (94%)
